description: Old Testament roots of the Messiah, the Son of Man title, and Jesus's baptism in Mark 1.
content_html:
Who Was the Messiah Supposed to Be?

At the time of Jesus, Jewish people in first-century Palestine were eagerly waiting for a Messiah. The Hebrew word means “anointed one” — the same concept as the Greek “Christ.” But expectations varied widely. Many Jews hoped for a warrior king like David who would overthrow Roman rule by military force. Others anticipated a priestly or prophetic figure. What almost nobody expected was a suffering Messiah who would die at the hands of the very oppressors he was meant to defeat.

One of the most important Old Testament passages Christians use to understand Jesus’s role is Isaiah 53. This text describes a “suffering servant” who is “despised and rejected” and who carries the people’s suffering in his own body. Early Christians read this passage and saw Jesus in it — the Messiah was not a conquering general but someone who fulfils God’s purposes through self-giving suffering. This is one reason why Mark’s Gospel, from its very opening lines, is so theologically charged.

Key Fact

Mark’s Gospel opens at Mark 1:1 with the declaration: “The beginning of the gospel about Jesus Christ, the Son of God.” Within the first eleven verses, Mark establishes Jesus as Messiah (Christ), Son of God, and the one who fulfils the prophecies of Isaiah. The Gospel then immediately goes on to announce Jesus’s baptism — his public commissioning as God’s chosen servant.

The Title ‘Son of Man’

One of the most unusual and distinctive titles Jesus uses for himself in Mark is Son of Man. Unlike “Messiah,” which carried powerful political overtones, “Son of Man” was more ambiguous and allowed Jesus to define his mission on his own terms. It has two layers of meaning.

The first layer comes from Daniel 7:13, which describes a heavenly figure “like a son of man” coming before God (“the Ancient of Days”) on clouds of glory and receiving “dominion and glory and a kingdom.” This apocalyptic figure has cosmic authority. When Jesus calls himself Son of Man, he is linking his identity to this heavenly ruler — a being with divine backing and an eternal kingdom.

The second layer is more human and vulnerable. Jesus also uses the title “Son of Man” when speaking of his coming suffering and death (for example when predicting his passion). This deliberate ambiguity is central to Mark’s portrayal of Jesus — he is simultaneously the exalted cosmic Lord of Daniel’s vision and the servant who must suffer. Scholars refer to this as the “hidden” nature of Jesus’s identity, and it runs throughout the whole Gospel.

At the time of Jesus, Jewish expectations of the Messiah were diverse. The Pharisees hoped for a teacher who would purify Jewish law. The Zealots wanted a military revolutionary. The Essenes (the community behind the Dead Sea Scrolls) anticipated a priestly Messiah from the tribe of Levi. Most of these groups would have been confused or even offended by Jesus, whose Messiah-ship centred on suffering, service and a cross rather than triumph.

Christians today see Isaiah 53 as proof that Jesus fulfilled Old Testament prophecy in an unexpected way — the “suffering servant” model reframes what messianic victory looks like. From a Humanist or atheist perspective, this reinterpretation is a post-hoc rationalisation: the early Christian community read its experience of Jesus’s death back into the Hebrew scriptures rather than fulfilling a genuine prediction.

The Baptism of Jesus (Mark 1:2–11)

Mark’s Gospel begins with extraordinary speed. There is no nativity story, no birth narrative, no genealogy. Mark immediately introduces John the Baptist, then launches straight into the baptism of Jesus (Mark 1:2–11). This reflects Mark’s breathless, urgent style — the word “immediately” appears over forty times in the Gospel.

In Mark 1:2–8, John the Baptist appears in the desert “preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.” Mark describes him wearing camel’s hair and eating locusts and wild honey — evoking the prophet Elijah. John declares that the one coming after him is so much greater that John is not even worthy to untie his sandals. This prepares the reader for the arrival of Jesus.

The baptism itself (Mark 1:9–11) contains three theologically significant moments. First, as Jesus comes up out of the water, the heavens are “torn open” — a dramatic, even violent image of God breaking into the world. Second, the Holy Spirit descends “like a dove” on Jesus — marking him as the one on whom the Spirit rests, recalling Isaiah’s description of the Spirit-filled servant. Third, a voice from heaven declares: “You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased.” This is a divine commissioning — God publicly identifies Jesus at the very beginning of his public ministry.

Key Fact

The baptism passage (Mark 1:9–11) contains a Trinitarian moment: the Father speaks from heaven, the Son is baptised in the water, and the Holy Spirit descends as a dove. This is significant for Christian understanding of Jesus as divine — the Father himself confirms Jesus’s identity.

John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance — people went to be washed of their sins. This raises an obvious question for Christians: why did a sinless Jesus submit to it? Different Christian traditions offer different answers. Some say Jesus was baptised in solidarity with sinful humanity — identifying with the people he came to save. Others argue he was submitting to God’s plan to show that all righteousness should be fulfilled. Still others focus on the baptism as a public commissioning for ministry rather than a washing from sin.

From a non-religious perspective, the baptism narrative is a significant historical problem. John’s baptism implied that Jesus needed to repent, which contradicts the Christian claim that Jesus was sinless. Many historians consider the baptism to be one of the most historically reliable events in the Gospels precisely because the early Church would not have invented something so potentially embarrassing. This is known as the “criterion of embarrassment.”

Significance for Christians Today

The titles Messiah, Son of Man and Son of God remain central to Christian identity and worship. Christians affirm Jesus as the Christ at baptism, in creeds, and in prayer. The suffering-servant model of the Messiah shapes Christian ethics: if the Son of God came to serve and suffer rather than to dominate, then Christian life is called to the same pattern of self-giving. The baptism of Jesus is also foundational for Christian sacramental practice — most Christian denominations celebrate baptism as a sacrament of initiation, modelled on Jesus’s own.
exam_tip_html: For “Explain two…” questions, make sure each explanation is developed — don’t just name the title or passage. For example, don’t just say “Jesus is called Son of Man” — explain what it meant and why it mattered. For the 5-mark question, remember the fifth mark depends on a named source: a book and passage (e.g. “In Daniel 7:13…” or “In Isaiah 53…”). For 12-mark Discuss questions, develop both sides fully — a common weakness is spending three paragraphs on the Christian view and one sentence on the Humanist or atheist response. SPaG marks are available on selected 12-mark questions — spell ‘Messiah’, ‘omnipotence’ and ‘apocalyptic’ correctly and use them precisely.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The title ‘Messiah’ means ‘anointed one’; Isaiah 53 presents a suffering servant model of messiahship that Christians see fulfilled in Jesus — at odds with popular Jewish expectations of a warrior king.
  • ‘Son of Man’ draws on Daniel 7:13 (cosmic authority) but also implies suffering; Jesus uses it as his preferred self-description in Mark, allowing him to define his own mission.
  • The baptism (Mark 1:9–11) is a divine commissioning: the Spirit descends, the Father speaks, and Jesus’s public ministry begins — giving Christians a Trinitarian basis for faith and a model for Christian baptism.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Old Testament expectations of the Messiah at the time of Jesus.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete points, e.g.:
• Many expected a warrior king in the tradition of David who would defeat Rome by force.
• Some hoped for a priestly figure who would restore pure worship in the Temple.
• Others anticipated a prophetic voice, like Elijah, calling the nation to repentance.
• Isaiah 53 describes a suffering servant — though this interpretation was not widely held before Jesus.

practice_questions.text: Describe the events of the baptism of Jesus as recorded in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points, e.g.:
• Jesus came from Galilee to be baptised by John in the River Jordan.
• As Jesus came up from the water, the heavens were 'torn open' and the Holy Spirit descended on him like a dove.
• A voice from heaven declared: 'You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased.'

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the baptism of Jesus is important for Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per reason: one for a basic point, two for a developed explanation.
• The baptism established Jesus's identity as the Son of God, confirmed by the Father's voice — this gives Christians confidence that Jesus truly was divine, supporting the doctrines of the Trinity and the Incarnation.
• The baptism models the Christian sacrament of baptism — since Jesus submitted to baptism himself, most denominations see it as the rite of initiation into the Church, marking the beginning of a Christian's life of faith.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the title 'Son of Man' helps Christians understand who Jesus is.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point (one for point, one for development), plus one mark for a named source:
• 'Son of Man' connects Jesus to Daniel 7:13, where a heavenly figure is given 'dominion and glory and a kingdom' by God — this shows Jesus as a cosmic figure with divine authority, not just a human teacher.
• Jesus also uses 'Son of Man' when predicting his own suffering and death, showing that the path to glory runs through sacrifice — this shapes Christian understanding of the cross as necessary and purposeful.
The fifth mark requires citing Daniel 7:13 (or Isaiah 53) as a named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Mark's Gospel presents Jesus mainly as a suffering servant rather than a triumphant Messiah.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; conclusion weighs the evidence and reaches a justified judgement.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least one named source; conclusion present.
Developing (4-6): One side more developed; few or no named sources; conclusion is descriptive.
Emerging (1-3): One-sided or very brief; minimal development.

Arguments in support: Isaiah 53 describes a 'suffering servant' — wounded for others' transgressions — which Christians apply to Jesus. The Son of Man title is used both for glory (Daniel 7:13) and for suffering/death. Mark's Gospel consistently shows the disciples failing to understand a Messiah who must suffer. The passion narrative is central to Mark's structure.
Arguments against: The baptism (Mark 1:9-11) presents a triumphant divine commissioning — the Father speaks, the Spirit descends. The Daniel 7:13 'Son of Man' is a figure of cosmic power and eternal kingship. The transfiguration (Mark 9:1-10) shows Jesus's divine glory. Mark ends with an empty tomb — resurrection implies triumph.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which John the Baptist prepared the way for Jesus in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• John preached in the desert, calling people to repent and be baptised for the forgiveness of sins.
• He pointed forward to a greater figure coming after him — someone so superior that John was not worthy to untie his sandals.
• He baptised Jesus in the River Jordan, at which point the Spirit descended and God identified Jesus as his Son.

knowledge_checks.q: Which Old Testament book contains the 'suffering servant' passage that Christians apply to Jesus as Messiah?
In Daniel 7:13, the 'Son of Man' is described as coming on the clouds to receive what from the Ancient of Days?
At the baptism of Jesus in Mark 1:9-11, the Holy Spirit descended on Jesus like a _____.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Title meaning 'anointed one' — the promised deliverer
Title drawn from Daniel 7:13 — Jesus's preferred self-description in Mark
Old Testament passage describing a suffering servant

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Hebrew word 'Messiah' mean?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Anointed one' — the same concept as the Greek 'Christ'.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Old Testament book and chapter describes a 'suffering servant' despised and rejected by others?
In which Old Testament passage does the 'Son of Man' receive dominion and a kingdom from God?
What two layers of meaning does the title 'Son of Man' carry in Mark's Gospel?
flashcard_questions.a: Cosmic authority (from Daniel 7:13) and suffering/death — both glory and the cross.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the first words of Mark's Gospel?
flashcard_questions.a: 'The beginning of the gospel about Jesus Christ, the Son of God.'

flashcard_questions.q: Who prepares the way for Jesus in Mark 1:2-8?
flashcard_questions.a: John the Baptist, preaching repentance in the desert.

flashcard_questions.q: What three things happened at Jesus's baptism in Mark 1:9-11?
flashcard_questions.a: The heavens tore open, the Spirit descended like a dove, and a voice declared 'You are my Son, whom I love.'

flashcard_questions.q: What did most first-century Jews expect the Messiah to do?
flashcard_questions.a: Overthrow Roman rule — a warrior king in the tradition of David.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Mark's Gospel described as having an 'urgent' or 'breathless' style?
flashcard_questions.a: The word 'immediately' appears over forty times — events follow each other rapidly.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'criterion of embarrassment' and why does it apply to the baptism?
flashcard_questions.a: Events unlikely to be invented (embarrassing to the early Church) are historically reliable; Jesus being baptised for repentance implies he needed it.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the baptism passage show the Trinity?
flashcard_questions.a: Father speaks from heaven, Son is baptised, Holy Spirit descends — all three persons present.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Isaiah 53 say about the suffering servant that Christians see fulfilled in Jesus?
flashcard_questions.a: He was 'despised and rejected', carried others' suffering, and was 'wounded for our transgressions'.

glossary_terms.definition: The promised deliverer whose coming was foretold in the Hebrew scriptures; the 'anointed one' of God.
A passage in the book of Isaiah describing a figure who suffers on behalf of others; Christians interpret it as a prophecy about Jesus.
A title Jesus uses of himself in Mark's Gospel, with roots in Daniel 7:13, where it describes a heavenly figure given authority by God.
An Old Testament book containing apocalyptic visions; Daniel 7:13 describes a figure 'like a son of man' coming on the clouds to receive authority from God.
A Jewish prophet who preached in the desert, calling people to repent and baptising them in the River Jordan; described as the forerunner of Jesus.
The period of Jesus's public teaching, healing and preaching activity, beginning after his baptism.
